passage: The photocopy shop outside the tehsil office in Shahabad was hot by noon, and so was the argument. Devika had found the cash box two hundred short again, and Wasim had just used the word "careless" about her accounts. Her voice rose. His did too. Then Wasim stopped, put both hands flat on the counter, and said, "I'm too angry to say anything useful. Give me one hour. I'll be back at one o'clock and we'll finish this." He walked to the canal bank and sat under the peepal tree. Devika watched him go, arms folded, half expecting him to disappear till night the way her uncle always did. At five to one, his cycle bell rang outside. He came in with two cups of tea.

qa.q: Where did Wasim go during the hour?
qa.a: He walked to the canal bank and sat under the peepal tree.

qa.q: How did Devika feel as she watched Wasim walk out?
qa.a: She felt wary and still angry, arms folded, half expecting him to disappear till night the way her uncle always did.

qa.q: What made Wasim's pause work instead of feeling like storming off?
qa.a: He named his anger, gave a clear return time, and came back at five to one, even bringing tea.

qa.q: What might Wasim have been going through as he sat under the peepal tree?
qa.a: Wasim was too angry to say anything useful, so he used the hour by the canal to calm down before coming back to finish the talk.

grounding: Shows a young man calling a stated time-out when too angry to talk well and coming back when he said he would.

passage: The argument in the tiny Valencia flat began over the heating bill and slid quickly into everything else. Beatriz was pacing; Ivan felt his jaw lock and heard himself about to say something about her mother. He stopped. "Bea, I'm too angry to talk well. Can we pick this up in an hour? Seven o'clock. I'm just going for a walk." She threw up her hands. "Great, just leave." "I'm coming back. Seven." He went down to the seafront and walked until his shoulders dropped. At six fifty-five, the key turned in the lock. He had two oranges from the corner shop and a calmer voice. Beatriz, who had spent the hour rehearsing how abandoned she felt, found she didn't need the speech.

qa.q: At what time did the key turn in the lock?
qa.a: The key turned in the lock at six fifty-five.

qa.q: What was Ivan worried he was about to say?
qa.a: He felt his jaw lock and sensed he was about to say something about Beatriz's mother, which he knew would do damage.

qa.q: Why did the stated return time matter so much here?
qa.a: Beatriz first heard the break as "just leave"; saying "seven" and keeping it turned a walkout into a pause she could trust.

qa.q: What was the hour like for Beatriz?
qa.a: She spent it feeling abandoned and rehearsing a speech, but his early return meant she no longer needed it.

grounding: Shows a partner asking for an hour's pause with a set return time and keeping it, so the break does not read as punishment.

passage:
In the electronics lab, the circuit had failed for the third time and the viva was tomorrow. Indu pointed at the breadboard. "You wired it wrong again, Shankar. I told you."
Shankar felt the heat rise up his neck. He put down the soldering iron very carefully. "I'm too angry to talk properly right now. Can we pick this up at four, after I take a walk?"
Indu blinked. "You're leaving?"
"I'm coming back. Four o'clock. Here."
He walked twice round the college ground and bought a lemon soda. At five to four he was back at the bench. Indu was already there, the circuit diagram open. "Okay," she said. "Show me your version."

qa.q: What time did Shankar say he would come back?
qa.a: At four o'clock.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he put the soldering iron down carefully?
qa.a: He felt angry and close to losing his temper, so he chose to pause before saying something harsh.

qa.q: Why did Shankar's pause work better than walking out?
qa.a: He named his anger, gave a clear return time and actually came back, so Indu did not read it as a punishment.

qa.q: What was Indu experiencing when Shankar said he was leaving?
qa.a: She was surprised and maybe worried he was walking out, but relieved when he came back on time.

grounding: In a college lab, a young man says he is too angry to talk well and asks to continue at a set time, then actually returns.

passage:
Shalini,

I'm writing this because I don't want last night to be the story of us.
When you said I only call when I need something, I felt like I was going to say something awful. So I said, "I'm too angry to talk well. Can I call you at nine?" and I hung up. I know that felt like a slammed door.
I went for a walk by the lake. I sat on the bench till my heart slowed down. At nine I called, like I said I would, and you picked up.
That call was better than any we've had this month. I want us to keep doing this: pause, name a time, come back.

Mridul

qa.q: Where did Mridul go during the pause?
qa.a: For a walk by the lake, then Mridul sat on the bench till the racing heart slowed.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when asking to call back at nine?
qa.a: Mridul felt so angry that saying something awful seemed close, and was afraid of that, so Mridul chose to pause.

qa.q: What makes Mridul's pause different from storming off?
qa.a: Mridul named the anger, gave a clear return time and called back at nine as promised, so it was a pause, not a punishment.

qa.q: What might Shalini have experienced when Mridul hung up?
qa.a: Shalini may have felt hurt and shut out at first, like a slammed door, and then relieved when the call came at nine as promised.

grounding: In a letter, a young adult describes calling a time-out with a stated return time and keeping that promise, which made the next talk better.

passage:
Okay, Kishore, you asked how me and my bandmate stopped fighting. I'm Yogesh, and honestly, I used to be the one who slammed doors.
Last month we were in the practice room, arguing about the setlist, and I felt that heat in my ears. I knew I'd say something about his singing that I couldn't take back.
So I said, "I'm too angry to talk well. Give me an hour. I'll be back at seven." He looked at me like, yeah right.
I walked to the tea stall and back twice. And at seven I walked in. He actually laughed, like he couldn't believe it.
That hour changed the whole fight. We sorted the setlist in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What were Yogesh and his bandmate arguing about?
qa.a: The setlist.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when the heat rose in his ears?
qa.a: He felt angry and afraid of saying something about his bandmate's singing that he couldn't take back.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's time-out work?
qa.a: He named his anger, gave a return time of seven and actually came back, so it didn't read as storming off.

qa.q: What was the bandmate experiencing when Yogesh walked in at seven?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and relieved, laughing because he hadn't believed Yogesh would really come back.

grounding: A young man tells a friend how he called a time-out with a return time instead of storming off, and came back to settle the argument.

passage:
I'm Rustom, the third person in this flat, so I was on the sofa when Wasim and Manoj really went at it about the rent split.

Voices up. Manoj said something about Wasim's "rich-boy habits." Wasim stood, red in the face, and I thought he was about to slam out like last time.

Instead he said, "I'm too angry to talk properly. Can we continue at nine? I'll be back." And he picked up his keys and left, closing the door normally.

Manoj just sat there. I could tell he didn't know what to do with it. Last time Wasim walked out, Manoj didn't sleep.

At 8:55 the lock turned. Wasim came in, put two chais on the table and said, "Okay. Let's try again."

I went to my room. Through the wall, I heard them talking, not shouting.

qa.q: What time did Wasim say they would continue?
qa.a: He said they would continue at nine.

qa.q: What might Wasim have been feeling when he stood up red in the face?
qa.a: He was probably very angry and hurt by the rich-boy remark, but he chose to pause rather than lash out or storm off.

qa.q: Why did Wasim's pause work better than walking out?
qa.a: He named the reason, gave a return time and came back on time, so Manoj could wait without feeling punished.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt while waiting for Wasim to come back?
qa.a: Manoj was probably unsettled and unsure, remembering the last walk-out, and likely relieved when Wasim returned with chai.

grounding: An observer watches one flatmate call a time-out with a return time and actually come back, unlike storming off.
